stories.title: Colliers Grows NYC Office, Industrial Leasing Teams With Two New Hires
stories.excerpt: Colliers is growing its New York City office and industrial leasing teams with two new hires, Commercial Observer has learned. Following a nearly seven-and-a-half-year tenure with Cushman & Wakefield, John Albal has joined Colliers as a senior associate within its Manhattan office and will focus on tenant representation and office leasing in Manhattan, according to Colliers. Meanwhile, Joseph Hentze Jr., a nearly six-year veteran at C&W, is joining the Manhattan office at Colliers as a vice president focusing on industrial leasing across the five boroughs. “John and Joseph bring valuable experience, strong client relationships and a deep understanding of the New York market to our team,” John Gallagher, executive managing director at Colliers in New York, said in a statement. “As companies continue to reassess their needs and make more strategic decisions about their real estate, having experienced advisers who can navigate an evolving market is more important than ever.” C&W declined CO’s request for comment. While Albal was with C&W, he specialized in tenant representation and advised C-suite executives regarding leasing opportunities and real estate strategies. “Colliers brings together a strong tenant representation business, deep market research and a respected global brand,” Albal said in a statement. “I’m excited to bring those resources to our clients and contribute to the firm’s continued growth in New York.” Hentze was most recently a director with C&W, where he advised both tenants and landlords on industrial leasing deals across Manhattan and the outer boroughs. “New York City’s industrial market presents a unique set of opportunities for businesses seeking space across the boroughs,” Hentze said in a statement. “I look forward to leveraging Colliers’ platform to help industrial owners and occupiers navigate their decisions and find properties that support their operational needs and long-term growth.&#82
bullets: Colliers hires two senior C&W brokers for NYC office and industrial leasing roles
Talent shift signals competitive repositioning as companies reassess real estate needs post-pandemic
No direct multifamily impact; office leasing market dynamics do not drive residential development
stories.summary: Colliers hired John Albal (senior associate, Manhattan office leasing) and Joseph Hentze Jr. (VP, five-borough industrial leasing) from Cushman & Wakefield. The move reflects Colliers' effort to capture advisory share in a market where companies are making more strategic real estate decisions. This is a service-sector talent migration with no bearing on multifamily supply, demand, or capital flows.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. Office brokerage consolidation does not signal shifts in residential demand, construction costs, or financing availability that would inform apartment acquisition or development strategy.

stories.title: Is Prop 45 a Quick Fix to California’s Slow Construction Pace?
stories.excerpt: The Golden State’s perpetual morass when it comes to quick development has been generating all the wrong kinds of headlines. In addition to the growing issues with housing production and affordability, it seems like any megaproject or big idea envisioned for California sinks due to red tape and regulations. The state’s perpetually delayed high-speed rail project continues to get pushed back. Recently, homebuilder Lennar went ahead with building homes on the site of the proposed rail line because land acquisition hadn’t taken place yet, nearly two decades into development. In Los Angeles, the 2.25-mile automated People Mover train has been delayed again, now stretching the project opening to early 2027, at a cost of $3.3 billion. The development has taken twice as long as it took to build the Golden Gate Bridge. The LAX Automated People Mover, also known as SkyLink, was scheduled to go into service in 2023. But the $3.5 billion project, has become bogged down in delays and contractural disputes, and remains in the testing phase. PHOTO: Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images That sense of being stuck has animated a campaign this year to pass Proposition 45, an effort to rework the state’s infamous California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to encourage more “essential infrastructure” and, in the words of advocates, streamline building and construction. Placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce and supported by big players in development, including homebuilders and the California Building Industry Association, the effort would designate certain projects as essential — including infrastructure like roads and bridges, certain kinds of housing, schools and broadband expansion — then impose time limits on environmental reviews and lawsuits to speed up approval and construction. This law would represent a “sea change,” said Ethan Elkind, a climate law expert at the Berkeley School of Law. Backers also argue it would be a windfall for the state
bullets: California Prop 45 seeks to streamline CEQA to accelerate essential infrastructure and housing projects
High-speed rail delays (20 years), LA People Mover ($3.3B, twice Golden Gate Bridge timeline) exemplify entitlement friction
Regulatory relief could reduce permitting timeline and soft costs, but passage and scope remain uncertain
stories.summary: Proposition 45 proposes amendments to California's Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite permitting for essential infrastructure and housing. The state's development timeline dysfunction—evidenced by the decades-long high-speed rail stall and the LA People Mover's $3.3 billion, 14+ year buildout—has constrained both public and private projects. If passed, Prop 45 could materially shorten entitlement cycles and reduce soft-cost burden on multifamily development in Los Angeles and statewide.
stories.impact: If Prop 45 passes, Los Angeles and California multifamily developers could see 12–24 month reductions in permitting and CEQA review, lowering pre-development risk and soft costs. However, regulatory relief alone does not solve land scarcity or construction-cost inflation; developers should monitor ballot language and implementation. This is a long-lead policy signal, not immediate capital or demand tailwind.

stories.title: Taiwan Chip Maker Eyes Fort Worth for $1.3B Plant
stories.excerpt: King Yuan Electronics, a Taiwanese semiconductor manufacturer, paid nearly $80 million for a cleanroom facility in Fort Worth. The company acquired the 27-acre property at 273 W. Everman Pkwy. The Everman Parkway location is part of the Fort Worth South Business Park. The company’s first U.S. manufacturing plant would be an estimated $1.3 billion investment that could create 630 jobs by the end of 2031. King Yuan’s plans call for the company to invest at least $1 billion in real property and $300 million in equipment. The company would conduct research and development, as well as testing, of semiconductors for next-generation GPUs and superchips. Additionally, it will provide testing services for Nvidia⁠. Wistron Corp.⁠ opened two supercomputer manufacturing plants worth $761 million in the AllianceTexas⁠ facility in Fort Worth this year as part of a partnership with the company. bullets: King Yuan Electronics invests $1.3B in Fort Worth semiconductor fab, creating 630 jobs by 2031
Taipei chipmaker paid $80M for 27-acre cleanroom facility; part of broader AI/GPU manufacturing cluster in Fort Worth South Business Park
Major employer inflow signals sustained job and population growth, strengthening multifamily rent growth runway in Fort Worth market
stories.summary: Taiwan's King Yuan Electronics paid ~$80 million for a 27-acre cleanroom facility in Fort Worth to build its first U.S. semiconductor manufacturing plant. The $1.3 billion investment—including $1B in real property and $300M equipment—will employ 630 direct workers by end of 2031 and provide GPU/superchip testing for Nvidia. This follows Wistron's $761 million supercomputer plant opening in AllianceTexas this year, anchoring a high-wage tech manufacturing cluster.
stories.impact: Fort Worth now emerging as critical AI/advanced manufacturing hub with two major Asian chipmakers investing >$2 billion in 2–3 years. This inflow of 1,000+ high-wage jobs will accelerate population in-migration and push renter demand and rent growth across Fort Worth proper and suburban corridors (especially near Alliance). Multifamily developers should prioritize acquisition near employment nodes and along commute corridors; expect rent premiums to reflect job growth trajectory through 2028–2031.

stories.title: Honeywell Planning $500M Phoenix Expansion
stories.excerpt: Honeywell Aerospace is spending $500 million on the 300,000-square-foot manufacturing plant, near its current site in Tempe. The company plans to break ground on the facility early next year, with completion slated for late 2028. When complete, the facility will include an integrated digital production system, modular robotics, automated inspection, digital twins, and will be powered by an end-to-end digital thread. The facility will support Honeywell Aerospace’s largest commercial and defense customers and most advanced products. Honeywell’s new Tempe facility will create 600 new jobs, and construction of the building is estimated to support 1,000 local jobs. Honeywell Aerospace is Arizona’s second-largest defense contractor. The company employs nearly 9,000 people in the metro area. It operates seven offices and manufacturing plants around the Phoenix area. The post Honeywell Planning $500M Phoenix Expansion appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Honeywell Aerospace commits $500M to 300K SF Tempe manufacturing facility; 600 direct jobs, 1,000 construction jobs
Groundbreaking early 2025, completion late 2028; Arizona's second-largest defense contractor expanding regional footprint
Sustained high-wage job growth in Phoenix metro bolsters multifamily demand, particularly suburban Tempe and East Valley corridors
stories.summary: Honeywell Aerospace is investing $500 million in a 300,000-square-foot advanced manufacturing plant near its existing Tempe site, with groundbreaking in early 2025 and completion by late 2028. The facility will create 600 permanent jobs and support 1,000 construction jobs. Honeywell already employs ~9,000 people across the Phoenix metro in seven locations and is the region's second-largest defense contractor.
stories.impact: Honeywell's $500M capex and job expansion reinforce Phoenix as a defense-aerospace-tech cluster with growing white-collar renter base. Multifamily developers should target Tempe and East Valley submarkets (e.g., Ahwatukee, Chandler, Tempe proper) to capture Honeywell's inbound talent through 2028 and beyond. Timing favors pre-delivery leasing windows and rent-growth positioning aligned with 2028–2029 absorption.

stories.title: Jason Maurer Joins SL Green as Managing Director
stories.excerpt: Jason Maurer has joined SL Green Realty, Manhattan’s largest office landlord, as a managing director. In his new role, Maurer will oversee retail leasing across the company’s portfolio, as well as lead office leasing for Green Property Services, SL Green’s third-party asset management platform, according to the firm. Maurer joins SL Green from Brookfield Properties, now known as BGRE. He joined the company as a vice president in 2018, according to his LinkedIn profile, and over the course of eight years rose to the dual roles of executive vice president and head of leasing for North America. Maurer’s two decades of retail and office leasing experience also includes roles at Newmark, Ripco Real Estate and General Growth Properties, spanning leasing strategy, portfolio positioning and mixed-use assets. “SL Green has long been one of the defining players in New York commercial real estate, with an institutional-quality portfolio and a depth of expertise that’s hard to replicate,” Maurer said in a statement. “What has impressed me is how entrepreneurial the company remains given that scale. I’m looking forward to bringing my experience across retail and office leasing to build on the strength of SL Green’s retail portfolio across New York while helping grow Green Property Services.” Green Property Services provides leasing and management services to properties owned by outside landlords. As of late September, the business operates across five buildings, totalling 1.3 million square feet. Maurer holds a bachelor’s degree in political science from the University of Michigan. After graduating in 2004, he joined Newmark Knight Frank, now Newmark, in its retail arm. He currently serves on the board of the Alliance for Downtown New York, Lower Manhattan’s business improvement district. A spokesperson for BGRE declined to comment on the news. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Jason Maurer joins SL Green as Managing Director, overseeing retail leasing and third-party office platform
20-year leasing veteran from Brookfield/BGRE; signals SL Green's strategic pivot toward asset management and portfolio services
No direct multifamily implication; office landlord staffing moves do not alter residential supply, demand, or financing
stories.summary: Jason Maurer, an 20-year leasing veteran who most recently served as EVP and head of North American leasing at Brookfield Properties (now BGRE), has joined SL Green Realty as Managing Director. He will oversee retail leasing across SL Green's Manhattan portfolio and lead office leasing for Green Property Services, the firm's third-party asset management platform. The hire reflects SL Green's strategic emphasis on retaining institutional-quality talent amid persistent office market challenges.
stories.impact: Immaterial to multifamily development. SL Green's office-leasing talent acquisition does not affect residential demand drivers, supply pipelines, or capital availability in any major multifamily market.

stories.title: Greystone Refis Hollywood, Fla., Apartments With $109M Loan
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between bti partners and Bridge Investment Group has secured a $109 million of agency debt to refinance a multifamily asset in Hollywood, Fla., Commercial Observer can first report. Greystone supplied the Freddie Mac-backed loan for the sponsorship’s 362-unit Bread Building property in Downtown Hollywood. BTI and Bridge acquired the property in 2021 for $11 million and redeveloped the former office building — which was once the headquarters for Hollywood Bread Company — into apartments. The conversion project was completed in 2025. “Utilizing Freddie Mac’s Lease-Up Loan program, we were able to provide the borrower with a cash-out refinance, full-term interest only, and 35-year amortization,” Richard Kourbage, senior managing director at Greystone, said in a statement. “The Bread Building’s successful lease-up and strong market fundamentals made it an excellent candidate for this financing.” The 25-story property reached full occupancy in September 2026, less than a year after conversion work was completed. The complex features roughly 17,000 square feet of retail space and 478 parking spaces. Cushman & Wakefield negotiated the debt with an equity, debt & structured finance team of Chris Moyer and Chris Lentz. “The Bread Building represented a compelling lending opportunity in one of South Florida’s most dynamic residential markets,” Moyer, executive managing director at Cushman & Wakefield, said in a statement. “The property’s prime location in the heart of Downtown Hollywood, proximity to major employment centers, and high-quality residential offerings allowed us to capitalize on the continued demand for luxury multifamily housing in South Florida.” Located at 1770 South Young Circle between Miami and Fort Lauderdale, the Bread Building is just south of ArtsPark at Young Circle, a 10-acre recreational green space. The property’s resident amenities include a swimming pool with cabanas, a sun deck, an outdoor kitchen and a fitness center
bullets: Greystone closes $109M Freddie Mac refi for 362-unit Bread Building adaptive-use conversion in Hollywood, Fla.
BTI Partners/Bridge Investment Group acquired for $11M (2021), converted former office HQ to apartments; reached full occupancy September 2026
35-year amortization, Freddie Mac lease-up program, cash-out refi signals agency appetite for conversion plays and South Florida multifamily
stories.summary: A joint venture between bti partners and Bridge Investment Group secured a $109 million Freddie Mac-backed loan to refinance the Bread Building, a 362-unit adaptive-use conversion of a former office building in Downtown Hollywood, Florida. The sponsors acquired the property in 2021 for $11 million and completed redevelopment in 2025. The property reached stabilization (full occupancy) in September 2026. Greystone structured the loan with 35-year amortization and full-term interest-only, using Freddie Mac's lease-up program.
stories.impact: South Florida multifamily remains well-capitalized; Freddie Mac's willingness to finance adaptive-use conversions at lease-up stage on 35-year terms signals strong agency appetite for Hollywood/Downtown Fort Lauderdale submarkets. Developers should monitor South Florida office-to-residential conversion economics: $11M acquisition (2021) + conversion costs yielding $109M refi implies strong value-add arbitrage and rent growth. This precedent supports pipeline development in secondary markets with aging office stock (e.g., Broward, Palm Beach).

stories.title: HSL Purchases 180-Unit Tucson Rental Community
stories.excerpt: HSL Properties paid $31.85 million for the Luma Apartments, a 180-unit project at 2600 W. Ina in Tucson, according to Real Estate Daily News. The sale comes out to just over $175,000 per unit. The seller was Village at The Foothills Owner LLC, of Beverly Hills, California, which can be traced to MC Residential in Scottsdale. Clint Wadlund and Hamid Panahi with Institutional Property Advisors (IPA) brokered the deal. Built in 1985, Luma Apartments comprises 21 two-story buildings on 16.33 acres. The community offers one- and two-bedroom apartments ranging from 757 to 1,158 square feet. Floor plans include one-bedroom, one-bath units; two-bedroom, one-bath units; and two-bedroom, two-bath units in two sizes. Amenities include two pools, a spa, pickleball, basketball and tennis courts, putting greens, picnic areas and a dog park. Residents also have access to a clubhouse, business center, lounge, and a fitness center. The post HSL Purchases 180-Unit Tucson Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: HSL Properties acquires Luma Apartments (180 units) in Tucson for $31.85M ($175.6K per unit) from MC Residential affiliate
Built 1985; 16.33 acres, fully amortized asset; sale reflects institutional consolidation in secondary markets
Per-unit pricing and age suggest stable, mature Tucson market with limited new development pressure and value-add upside from operations
stories.summary: HSL Properties purchased Luma Apartments, a 180-unit community in Tucson built in 1985, for $31.85 million (~$175,600 per unit). The seller was a Beverly Hills entity traceable to MC Residential in Scottsdale. The property comprises 21 two-story buildings across 16.33 acres and includes one- and two-bedroom units, two pools, fitness center, and recreational courts. The sale represents a typical institutional portfolio transaction in a mature secondary market.
stories.impact: Low relevance to new development strategy. Tucson per-unit valuations (~$176K) reflect a mature, built market with limited new-supply pressure. Developers eyeing Tucson should focus on land acquisitions or infill opportunities rather than acquisition of 40+ year-old assets; the cap rate and return profile on this type of stabilized asset offer limited leverage to growth stories in higher-demand metros (Phoenix, Austin, Denver).

stories.title: Walmart Advancing $400M San Antonio-Area Distribution Center
stories.excerpt: Walmart is moving ahead on a $400 million distribution center in Cibolo, a San Antonio suburb. The company says work on the 744,000-square-foot store could begin early next year, with completion slated for the third quarter in 2029. ESI Group is designing the project. Commercial Search reports the city approved a 75 percent property tax abatement running for 10 years and a 50 percent rebate of the maintenance and operations property tax for five years, as well as a performance-based sales tax. This amounts to roughly $32.5 million in tax breaks. Additionally, the council established a tax increment reinvestment zone in the area. The facility will rise on 126 acres at 3641 S. Santa Clara Road, the former San Antonio Raceway site along Interstate 10 in Guadalupe County. This industrial submarket has an industrial vacancy of 5 percent as of September. Walmart operates 38 stores in the San Antonio metro area. In Texas, the company operates 22 supply chain facilities. The post Walmart Advancing $400M San Antonio-Area Distribution Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Walmart advances $400M distribution center in Cibolo, San Antonio suburb; 744K SF, 1,000 construction + permanent jobs
Groundbreaking early 2025, delivery Q3 2029; city grants 75% property tax abatement (10 yr), 50% M&O rebate (5 yr), ~$32.5M total incentives
Industrial submarket at 5% vacancy (Sept 2024); major employer capex will drive logistics talent and population spillover to residential markets
stories.summary: Walmart is investing $400 million in a 744,000-square-foot distribution center in Cibolo, a San Antonio suburb, with groundbreaking expected early 2025 and completion Q3 2029. The city approved $32.5 million in incentives, including a 75% property tax abatement for 10 years and 50% maintenance-and-operations rebate for 5 years. The facility will rise on 126 acres (former San Antonio Raceway site) in an industrial submarket with 5% vacancy as of September 2024. Walmart operates 38 stores in the metro and 22 supply chain facilities in Texas.
stories.impact: Walmart's $400M capex and 1,000+ jobs (construction + permanent) will anchor logistics and blue-collar workforce expansion in the San Antonio metro, particularly Cibolo and north-side corridors. Multifamily developers should target workforce housing (Class B/C, 1–2 bed, affordable to moderate rents) near I-10 and logistics clusters; expect rent growth in these submarkets as Walmart and other supply-chain firms compete for workers. This is a 4–5 year build cycle, offering a medium-term demand tailwind for logistics-adjacent residential.

stories.title: ARCTRUST, Edison Equity Teaming Up on 175-Unit Austin-Area 55+ Community
stories.excerpt: ARCTRUST Private Capital and Edison Equity Residential broke ground on Serenova at Dripping Springs, a 175-residence, 55+ age-restricted community in Dripping Springs, Texas. The groundbreaking follows the August closing of the project’s construction loan, provided by North River Partners. This project follows the duo’s effort on Serenova at Woodforest, which broke ground in October 2025. Located adjacent to the Headwaters master-planned community, Serenova at Dripping Springs will include 133 upscale one- and two-bedroom apartment homes and 42 private villas. Serenova at Dripping Springs concierge services will include personal assistance with reservations, travel, in-home needs and social planning. Planned amenities include a chef-curated restaurant and social bar, wellness-focused fitness centers, a pool, a creative arts studio, a club room, a community lounge and marketplace,. With construction now underway, the first residents are anticipated in Fall 2028. The project team includes Market Square Architects, StudioSIX5 Design and The Brownstone Group. The post ARCTRUST, Edison Equity Teaming Up on 175-Unit Austin-Area 55+ Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: ARCTRUST/Edison Equity breaks ground on Serenova at Dripping Springs (175 units, 55+ age-restricted) in Austin suburb
North River Partners provided construction financing; first residents fall 2028; part of broader Serenova 55+ platform (Woodforest site also active)
Dripping Springs population and affluent retiree inflow signal sustained demand for upscale senior housing in high-growth Austin meta
stories.summary: ARCTRUST Private Capital and Edison Equity Residential broke ground on Serenova at Dripping Springs, a 175-residence 55+ age-restricted community in Dripping Springs, Texas. The project includes 133 one- and two-bedroom apartments and 42 private villas. North River Partners provided construction financing (closed August 2024). First residents are anticipated Fall 2028. The development is positioned adjacent to the Headwaters master-planned community and is part of a broader Serenova 55+ platform (including Serenova at Woodforest, which broke ground October 2025).
stories.impact: Austin metro's affluent population growth and aging demographic tail are driving upscale 55+ senior housing development in suburban nodes (Dripping Springs, Woodforest). Both projects signal operator confidence in rent growth and market absorption through late 2020s. Multifamily developers should monitor Dripping Springs and comparable Austin exurban corridors for acquisition/development of market-rate and affordable workforce housing to capture spillover demand from logistics, tech, and professional services job growth. Senior housing success validates pricing power in affluent submarkets.

stories.title: Lightstone Capital Provides $29.5M Loan for Orange, N.J., Multifamily Development
stories.excerpt: Orange, N.J.-based PEEK Capital, a division of multifamily developer and operator PEEK Properties, has secured a $29.5 million bridge loan on its recently completed multifamily project in Orange known as the Lincoln, Commercial Observer has learned. The bridge loan was provided by Lightstone Group’s real estate debt platform, Lightstone Capital. Daniel Cohen of Ackman-Ziff advised on the transaction. “Peek Properties is a best-in-class sponsor, and Lightstone executed flawlessly on this pre-stabilization bridge loan, which allowed Peek to repatriate equity early in the leasing process,” Cohen told CO in a statement. The loan will support the 102-unit building’s continued lease-up and stabilization, as well as refinance the property’s previous construction financing. Peek previously secured a $20.5 million loan for the development from Amboy Bank in 2024, Real Estate NJ reported. The five-story, full-block apartment building at 407 Highland Avenue in Orange received its final certificate of occupancy in September, according to Lightstone Capital, and has begun leasing a range of one- and two-bedroom residences. “Newly built multifamily properties with proven sponsorship track records have always presented attractive lending opportunities as they transition towards stabilization,” Eugene Rozovsky, senior managing director at Lightstone Capital, said in a statement. The property’s location is one black from N.J. Transit’s Highland Avenue station, offering access to Newark and Midtown Manhattan’s Pennsylvania Station. The cities of Orange and East Orange have been a popular site of luxury apartment development for several years, as renters are priced out of New York City. “The Lincoln continues to attract strong interest from prospective residents, and this refinancing marks an important milestone in the life cycle of the property,” Philip J. bullets: PEEK Capital secures $29.5M bridge loan from Lightstone Capital for 102-unit Lincoln in Orange, New Jersey (pre-stabilization)
Project completed with final CO September 2024; bridge refinances prior Amboy Bank $20.5M construction loan; supports lease-up
Orange, N.J. multifamily financing signals bridge-loan appetite for stabilizing urban infill projects in close-in Northeast urban markets
stories.summary: PEEK Properties (via PEEK Capital) secured a $29.5 million bridge loan from Lightstone Capital for the Lincoln, a 102-unit multifamily project in Orange, New Jersey. The full-block, five-story building received its final certificate of occupancy in September 2024 and is in active lease-up. The bridge loan refinances prior construction financing (Amboy Bank, $20.5 million in 2024) and supports ongoing stabilization. Daniel Cohen of Ackman-Ziff advised on the transaction.
stories.impact: Orange, N.J. urban multifamily development demonstrates bridge lender appetite for pre-stabilization refinances in close-in Northeast infill markets, especially when sponsored by established operators (PEEK Properties). Developers pursuing similar urban redevelopment plays in secondary Northeast metros (Newark, Jersey City, Hartford, Providence) should model bridge-to-permanent refinance timelines aligned with 9–12 month lease-up. Lightstone's activity signals healthy competition for institutional-grade bridge debt, supporting faster equity repatriation and lower carry costs for sponsors.
